reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: Long-term lithium therapy causes a chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy with slowly progressive renal impairment
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is the earliest and commonest renal effect, with polyuria, polydipsia and impaired urinary concentration
Biopsy typically shows tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis and characteristic distal tubular and collecting-duct microcysts
Lithium enters collecting-duct principal cells via the epithelial sodium channel and interferes with aquaporin-2 water channels, causing resistance to antidiuretic hormone
Nephrotoxicity relates to cumulative dose and duration, so the decision to continue lithium must balance renal risk against psychiatric benefit
Distinguish chronic nephropathy from acute lithium toxicity, which can cause acute kidney injury and neurotoxicity, sometimes requiring dialysis
Management centres on drug withdrawal and supportive care where feasible, careful monitoring, and adequate hydration, with a specialist mental-health discussion before stopping
reference.pathophysiology: Lithium is freely filtered and reabsorbed in the proximal tubule and enters collecting-duct principal cells through the epithelial sodium channel. Within these cells it disrupts signalling and downregulates aquaporin-2 water channels, impairing the antidiuretic response and producing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Chronic exposure injures the distal nephron and collecting ducts, driving tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis and the formation of distal tubular and collecting-duct microcysts, which correlate with progressive loss of glomerular filtration. Some patients also develop a distal renal tubular acidification defect and, less commonly, proteinuria. The cumulative burden of exposure determines the degree of irreversible chronic damage.
additionalDifferentials: Other chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathies (analgesic, aristolochic acid)
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (given microcysts)
additionalInvestigations: Serum lithium level and review of cumulative exposure and duration
Renal function trend and estimated glomerular filtration rate
Urine osmolality with a water-deprivation and desmopressin assessment for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Renal ultrasound or MRI, which may show microcysts
Renal biopsy in selected cases to confirm chronic tubulointerstitial disease
redFlags: Acute lithium toxicity with neurological features and acute kidney injury
Severe hypernatraemia from uncontrolled nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Rapidly declining renal function suggesting an additional insult
Volume depletion precipitating lithium accumulation and toxicity
reference.prognosis: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and early functional changes are often partly reversible if lithium is stopped, but established interstitial fibrosis and reduced glomerular filtration may be irreversible and can progress even after discontinuation, occasionally to end-stage kidney disease. Careful monitoring and shared decision-making about continuing therapy improve long-term renal outcomes.
pitfalls: Stopping lithium abruptly without psychiatric input, risking relapse of mood disorder
Attributing polyuria to primary polydipsia rather than nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Allowing volume depletion or NSAID use that precipitates lithium toxicity
Assuming renal impairment will reverse fully once the drug is withdrawn
Confusing lithium microcysts with polycystic kidney disease on imaging
management: Review the ongoing need for lithium with psychiatry, weighing renal risk against relapse risk, and consider switching to an alternative mood stabiliser
Use the lowest effective lithium exposure and avoid toxic peaks if the drug is continued
Treat lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with amiloride, which blocks principal-cell uptake via the epithelial sodium channel, ensuring free access to water
Avoid nephrotoxic and interacting drugs (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides) and maintain hydration, especially during intercurrent illness
Monitor renal function, lithium levels and urinary concentrating ability, and manage any distal renal tubular acidification defect
Apply general chronic kidney disease measures including blood-pressure control and cardiovascular risk reduction
Refer to nephrology, planning renal replacement therapy if disease progresses towards end-stage kidney failure
